content: RalB, or Ras-related protein Ral-B, is a protein encoded by the RALB gene located on chromosome 2 in humans. It belongs to the Ras GTPase family and is one of two paralogs of the Ral protein, the other being RalA. RalB functions as a molecular switch, becoming active when bound to GTP and inactive when bound to GDP. This protein plays a critical role in regulating various biological processes, including cell division, intracellular transport, and signaling pathways. Its involvement in these processes has been implicated in the progression of several cancers. Structurally, RalA and RalB share an 80% similarity in their amino acid sequences and are identical in their effector-binding regions. However, they differ significantly in their C-terminal hypervariable regions, which contain multiple sites for post-translational modifications. These modifications influence their subcellular localization and biological functions. For instance, phosphorylation of serine 194 on RalA by the kinase Aurora A causes RalA to relocate to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it facilitates mitochondrial fission. In contrast, phosphorylation of serine 198 on RalB by protein kinase C (PKC) directs RalB to other internal membranes, activating its tumorigenic functions. RalB interacts with components of the exocyst complex, such as Exo84 and Sec5, to mediate processes like autophagosome assembly, secretory vesicle trafficking, and tethering. It also participates in exocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis, tight junction biogenesis, filopodia formation, mitochondrial fission, and cytokinesis. While many of these functions are shared with RalA, the distinct subcellular localizations of the two isoforms result in their differential involvement in specific biological processes. Notably, RalB is more prominently associated with apoptosis and cell motility. Additionally, RalB interacts with Exo84 to assemble the Beclin-1–VPS34 autophagy initiation complex and with Sec5 to activate the innate immune response via Tank-binding kinase 1 (TBK1). Clinically, Ral proteins, including RalB, are associated with the progression of various cancers, such as bladder and prostate cancer. Although the precise mechanisms remain unclear, studies suggest that RalB promotes tumor invasion and metastasis. Inhibiting RalB has been shown to suppress cancer progression. Furthermore, RalB regulates p53 levels in a K-Ras-independent manner during cancer development. It also enhances cell survival during infections by double-stranded DNA viruses by activating TBK1 to initiate an immune response. RalB has been demonstrated to interact with several proteins, including CDC42, EXOC8, RALBP1, and Sec5. These interactions further underscore its multifaceted roles in cellular processes and its significance in both normal physiology and disease states.
